title: 1 Timothy 3:14–16
context: Paul explains why he is writing: so Timothy will know how to conduct himself in God’s household, the church that upholds the truth. He then cites what may be an early hymn about Christ, tracing his path from incarnation to ascension. Church order rests on the person and work of Christ.

voices.heading: Voices from both camps
voices.intro: On God’s household and the mystery of godliness, a few classic voices from each tradition.
voices.note: Quotations lightly abridged for length; wording follows standard English translations of the sources named.

arminian.quote: The church of the living God—opposed to the temple of Diana. The mystery of godliness—The whole mystery of true religion, the mystery of the gospel, the mystery of Christ. God was manifested in the flesh—In the human nature. Justified by the Spirit—Declared to be the Son of God with power. Seen of angels—Who worshipped him. Preached among the Gentiles. Believed on in the world. Received up into glory.
arminian.source: Explanatory Notes upon the New Testament (on 1 Tim 3:15–16)

reformed.quote: The church is the pillar and foundation of the truth, not because the truth derives its authority from the church, but because the church is the guardian and witness of the truth. Without controversy, great is the mystery of godliness: God was manifested in the flesh. Here is the sum of the gospel, which both learned and unlearned ought to acknowledge.

verses.text: These things I write to you, hoping to come to you shortly,
verses.arminianNotes:
Hope of coming soon, and still he writes. Presence is preferred; a letter is love when delayed.

For the hearer: instruction for the household does not wait on the apostle’s travel plans. Written apostolic teaching is already a gift to a church that must behave before he arrives.
verses.reformedNotes:
I hope to come / I am writing so that: delay is anticipated, truth is not postponed.

God uses a letter to order His house. The so that of v. 15 is why ink is also ministry.

verses.text: but if I wait long, that you may know how men ought to behave themselves in God’s house, which is the assembly of the living God, the pillar and ground of the truth.
verses.arminianNotes:
If I delay: Timothy must know how men ought to behave. Household of God, assembly of the living God, pillar and ground of the truth—three names for one people. Wesley contrasted the living God with Diana’s temple.

Both camps stand together here: the church does not author the truth; she holds it up. Behavior in the house matches the God who lives there. This is shared ecclesiology more than a soteriology fight.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: pillar and foundation not because truth derives authority from the church, but because the church is guardian and witness. Household of the living God.

Reformed and Arminian readers can say this in one voice: conduct in God’s house is not casual, and the truth has a people who buttress it without becoming its source.

verses.text: Without controversy, the mystery of godliness is great: God was revealed in the flesh, justified in the spirit, seen by angels, preached among the nations, believed on in the world, and received up in glory.
verses.arminianNotes:
Great indeed, we confess: a shared hymn. He—Christ—manifested in flesh, justified in the spirit, seen by angels, preached among the nations, believed on in the world, and received up in glory. Wesley called this the whole mystery of true religion, the mystery of Christ.

Do not force a camp fight the verse is not staging. Classical Arminians and Reformed Christians confess this together: incarnation, vindication, cosmic witness, global proclamation, faith in the world, and exaltation. Godliness has a mystery, and the mystery is a Person, not a party platform.
verses.reformedNotes:
Calvin: here is the sum of the gospel, which learned and unlearned ought to acknowledge. God manifested in the flesh.

Reformed confession stands on the same six lines. Election and resistible grace are not the point of this verse; the risen Christ is. The nations, the world, and glory are the hymn’s geography—shared ground under both pulpits.
